## Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author)

This paper uses a global dataset of fossil pollen, paleoclimate, archaeologically-attested radiocarbon dates and human indicator pollen types to investigate the relative importance of humans and climate on aspects of pollen diversity and compositional changes from 8.5 cal k BP onwards. Previous work has described changes to various aspects of pollen diversity and compositional turnover measures over multi-millennial timescales across much of the earth surface. Other studies have investigated the relative strengths of relationships between humans versus climate on pollen diversity and compositional turnover for different continents and regions. However, this study represents the first attempt to quantify the relative importance of humans and climate on pollen diversity and compositional turnover measures at a global scale in the Holocene. Using a new method to the field of paleoecology, the authors claim that, at continental and regional scales, climate was the primary driver of pollen diversity and compositional turnover measures over the period 8 - 2.5cal k BP. This work adds a novel dimension to the conversation (a direct comparison of the strength of drivers globally) and thus represents an interesting and worthwhile contribution to the literature.

> **Response.** We thank the reviewer for recognising the scope of the study and for identifying where the ecological evidence and its limitations required clearer explanation. We now refer consistently to pollen assemblage dynamics, define 8.5–2.0 ka BP as the interval supported by the principal archaeological comparison, and show younger expert-derived events separately. Histories of the pollen assemblage properties now precede the comparison of climate and human activity, and the revised Methods and Discussion give fuller attention to the construction, spatial meaning, and limitations of each source of evidence.

I do, however, have a number of data presentation and methodological concerns that I would need to see addressed to have confidence in the results presented here. I also see no advantage of including the human event variable here. I understand that the authors would prefer to be able to run these analyses up to the present, but I find the variable reductive and without nuance, it is un-tested and it is much too coarse for it to ever be likely to capture changes to local PAPs. In addition to methodological considerations, I would also like to see an adjustment to the title. In its current form, at least to me, the title suggests that this is a study encompassing the full Holocene, though the primary analyses span the period 8.5 - 2 cal k BP. This is very important because recent work has shown substantial increases in multiple measures of pollen diversity from 2.5 cal k BP onwards across the planet (e.g. in Europe, Giesecke et al, 2019; North America, Stegner and Spanbauer, 2023; global, Mottl et al, 2021 and Gordon et al, 2024), a period of known rapid and major change in human population size, culture, etc. These changes are missed in these analyses given the cut-off date. Climate outweighs human effects on vegetation assemblage dynamics 8 - 2.5 ka BP (or similar) would seem to me to be a more accurate and less ambiguous representation of the analyses.

> **Response.** We agree that the former title overstated both the temporal extent and the ecological domain of the study. The revised title is “Climate outweighs human effects on pollen assemblage dynamics from 8.5 to 2.0 ka BP,” and the conclusion is explicitly restricted to this interval. The expert event chronology is too coarse to represent the full diversity of local human activity, but we have retained it as secondary historical evidence. It documents regionally interpreted indications of disturbance and land use that may be absent from archaeological SPDs and, in some regions, extends into younger periods. Comparing the two sources shows whether the broad conclusion depends on how human activity is represented. SPD remains the principal proxy, and the event chronology is not treated as independent confirmation because it partly derives from the same pollen archive as the ecological response.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The title, Abstract, hypotheses, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion now define the principal interval as 8.5–2.0 ka BP. Younger event observations are labelled separately in Fig. 4. The Methods and Supplementary Information explain the different historical evidence represented by SPDs and expert-interpreted pollen events.

### Data presentation

Though two records are presented in Extended Fig. 3, a key figure missing from this work is a presentation of the full set of PAPs through time for each region. The authors have presented the set of predictor variables, rather than the response variables, which, in my view, are of substantially less importance than the response variables themselves. I find it difficult to make sense of and interpret statistical analyses for which at least some abstraction of the response variables (here, PAPs) are not presented in a paper and thus, for me, these need to be included.

> **Response.** We agree that the histories of the pollen assemblage properties should be visible before their possible drivers are considered. We have therefore moved the descriptive trajectories ahead of the H1 results. Fig. 2 brings together six properties spanning richness, diversity, compositional change, and change-point density; Supplementary Figs. S12–S21 show all ten properties individually for each region within the continental groups. The shaded intervals convey uncertainty in the modelled trajectories, and gaps indicate where the contributing sequences do not provide sufficient temporal coverage. Each sequence contributes equally over its observed interval, so a long or densely sampled sequence does not dominate a regional curve. Together, these figures show both broad temporal tendencies and substantial variation among regions, providing ecological context for the subsequent comparison of climate and human activity.

> The regional curves are not response data for either H1 analysis. In the spatial analysis, HVarPart is fitted to PAP values within each individual fossil pollen sequence, and the resulting contributions are summarised across sequences only afterward. In the temporal analysis, PAP values from individual sequences enter 500-year continental-group time slices, with spatial structure among those sequences represented in the model. Neither analysis uses the plotted regional summary curves as its response. The [full collection of figures for eligible individual sequences](https://github.com/HOPE-UIB-BIO/PastHumanImpact/tree/f16590d7d6c68fdfae99e5286af01ab2f7a6e807/Outputs/Figures/Dataset_trends) is available on GitHub for inspection; the number of figures makes their inclusion in the Supplementary Information impractical.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Results now begin with “Temporal patterns in pollen assemblage properties.” Fig. 2 and Supplementary Figs. S12–S21 present descriptive regional trajectories. The Methods explicitly distinguish these displays from the sequence-level PAP values used in H1.

For ease of assessment, we reproduce the ten supplementary PAP figures below. They are descriptive summaries of sequence-level trajectories; the H1 models use PAP values from individual sequences, as explained above.

### Pollen diversity biases

Whether implicitly or explicitly stated, pollen data in studies such as these are used to make inferences on the changing diversity patterns, and relationships with drivers, of the parent vegetative assemblages of pollen samples (as stated by the authors, L652). Thus, the treatment of the pollen data in order to make robust inferences about the actual focus – the parent vegetative assemblage – is of paramount importance. For the reasons outlined below, the treatment of the pollen data in these analyses means that I find it difficult to have full confidence in the robustness of the computed PAPs and thus confidence in the conclusions of this work.

There is substantial variation in pollen productivity among pollen producing plants, which has the capacity to strongly bias estimates of individual PAPs, which the authors acknowledge (L687). Pollen grains from high pollen producing plants are more likely to be deposited and identified in pollen samples than pollen grains from low pollen producing plants. The result is that at low pollen sums, pollen assemblages (samples) are likely to be swamped by pollen grains from a relatively smaller number of high pollen producing plants. This means that the evenness of these samples will be low (high representation by a small number of types), the result of which is a reduced likelihood of detecting pollen types from other pollen producers, which thus artificially depresses the richness of these samples (e.g. Giesecke et al, 2014). Thus at low pollen sums, the richness of samples primarily reflects the evenness of those samples. Similarly, if the likelihood of sampling a diverse set of grains per sample is reduced (given the low evenness of samples), compositional turnover estimates are likely to be lower for these samples than between samples with higher evenness values. In these analyses, pollen samples are rarefied to either 150 or 25 pollen grains. Even 150 grains is substantially lower than the minimum rarefaction value of ~300-500 grains commonly used in pollen diversity analyses. For those samples rarefied to 25 grains, diversity estimates will almost certainly be affected strongly by these confounding issues. Extended Fig. 3 describes the PAPs and predictor variables for two records, where these described issues can clearly be seen: those Hill numbers N0, N1 and N2 (~richness, ~diversity and ~evenness) are strongly correlated.

These concerns can be at least partly mitigated against by performing some transformation of pollen counts based on relative pollen production and dispersal (etc). There are a number of methods to achieve this, the most notable of which is the REVEALS model, for which there are the requisite datasets for many of the regions used here. However, this is not implemented in these analyses. At the very minimum, I would expect to see a supplementary analysis that considers only the subset of samples and records with a substantially higher minimum pollen grain N (300-500 grains), to check that results are not driven by those issues relating to relative differences in pollen production and dispersal described above. I am of the view that all samples with <150 grains should be excluded from these analyses.

> **Response.** We agree that pollen productivity, dispersal, taxonomic resolution, basin setting, and count size all influence the ecological meaning of pollen assemblage properties. Low counts can make uncommon pollen types less likely to be detected and can affect estimates of richness, evenness, and compositional change. These properties are therefore interpreted as features of the recovered pollen assemblage rather than direct estimates of plant abundance or vegetation diversity. A minimum of 25 terrestrial grains determines whether an individual count-based sample can be retained; it is not a common rarefaction target imposed on every sample. A count-based sequence is retained only when more than half of its samples in the study interval have at least 150 grains. The usual rarefaction target is 150 grains, with a lower sequence-specific target where a retained sequence cannot consistently support 150. This rule limits the contribution of low-count samples while preserving sequences from less well represented regions; it does not remove the uncertainty associated with smaller counts.

> We examined what would be lost if more demanding count criteria were applied to the `r format(preparation_pool_n, big.mark = ",")` prepared sequences. A 300-grain rarefaction target, paired with a 50-grain sample minimum, retains `r pollen_retention |> filter(.data[["threshold"]] == 300) |> pull(.data[["n_records_retained"]])` sequences. A 500-grain target, paired with a sample minimum of about 83 grains, retains `r pollen_retention |> filter(.data[["threshold"]] == 500) |> pull(.data[["n_records_retained"]])`; a 1,000-grain target, paired with a minimum of about 167 grains, retains only `r pollen_retention |> filter(.data[["threshold"]] == 1000) |> pull(.data[["n_records_retained"]])`. The 500-grain scenario therefore removes `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pollen_retention[["prop_lost"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 500])`% of baseline sequences and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pollen_retention[["prop_samples_lost"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 500])`% of their samples; the 1,000-grain scenario removes `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pollen_retention[["prop_lost"]][pollen_retention[["threshold"]] == 1000])`% of sequences. The losses differ among continental groups, so higher count requirements would come at the cost of a narrower and less geographically representative historical archive. Supplementary Fig. S23A shows the observed count distribution in count-based samples, while Fig. S23B shows that the loss of sequences and samples differs markedly among continental groups. We retain the baseline rule on that basis while acknowledging the greater uncertainty of PAP estimates from smaller counts.

> This diagnostic concerns the availability of pollen evidence under different thresholds. It does not meet the reviewer’s proposed robustness test in full: we did not refit H1 after requiring every sample to contain 300–500 grains, and the figure does not show that the estimated climate and human contributions would remain unchanged under such a restriction. The response to pollen-production and dispersal differences also remains incomplete without a comparable correction across regions.

> Correlation among the PAP responses does not itself invalidate the multivariate H1 analysis. Ecological community analyses routinely consider species whose abundances covary; their response variables need not be mutually independent. Richness, evenness, and the Hill-number measures likewise describe related aspects of the same pollen assemblages. Their overlap could give some dimensions of assemblage change greater weight, so we measured it rather than assuming it was inconsequential. Supplementary Fig. S24 shows the actual PAP correlations: `r pap_correlation_strong_n` of `r pap_correlation_pairs_n` pairs have a median absolute correlation of at least 0.8 across eligible groups.

> We then repeated the spatial SPD H1 analysis with a reduced, less redundant PAP response. Among `r format(pap_paired_climate[["n_pairs"]], big.mark = ",")` sequences estimable in both configurations, the median signed climate contribution ratio changed from `r sprintf("%.3f", pap_paired_climate[["median_baseline"]])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", pap_paired_climate[["median_reduced"]])`, and the median signed human contribution ratio changed from `r sprintf("%.3f", pap_paired_human[["median_baseline"]])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", pap_paired_human[["median_reduced"]])`. Supplementary Fig. S30 shows the reduced-response climate–human pattern. Climate retains the larger estimated contribution in the aggregate; changes for individual sequences remain visible and should not be described as identical results.
> We did not apply REVEALS because the pollen-productivity estimates, dispersal parameters, basin descriptions, and taxonomic resolution needed for a comparable analysis are not available across all regions. Restricting that correction to Europe or other well-studied regions would make the ecological meaning of the response differ among continental groups. The revised article therefore treats productivity and dispersal as unresolved limitations and does not imply that rarefaction corrects them.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The count procedure and the relationships among pollen assemblage properties are now explained in the Methods. The Supplementary Information shows the loss of geographical and temporal coverage under stricter targets, the observed correlations among properties in Fig. S24, and the reduced-response climate–human result in Fig. S30. The Discussion contains a dedicated account of how pollen production, dispersal, and finite counts constrain ecological interpretation.

For direct assessment, we reproduce the observed PAP correlations and the climate–human result obtained with a less redundant response set.

### SPD biases

SPDs of archaeologically attested radiocarbon dates are becoming increasingly used to infer relative changes in human paleodemography. However, there is substantial and ongoing debate in the literature among archaeologists about whether this method can actually tell us anything about paleodemography (e.g. Chaput and Gajewski, 2016; Crema and Bevan, 2020; Crema, 2022) . It is only material from times and places of archaeological interest that are radiocarbon dated. Thus the number of radiocarbon dated objects through time and space is intensely non-random, clustering around locations and periods of interest to the archaeological community. This is likely the cause of the substantial apparent paleodemographic spikes during transitions between archaeological periods (archaeologists are interested in what caused and was affected by these transitions). On top of this, radiocarbon dating is expensive. So, when possible, other objects – e.g., pottery, coins – are preferentially used to date archaeological remains, which results in a reduction in the number of radiocarbon dates when these objects are readily available. This is most obviously shown in Europe from ~3 cal k BP, from which point the radiocarbon SPD shows a monotonic decline (Extended Data Fig. 4). This apparent reduction is entirely artificial and driven by the general cessation of the use of radiocarbon dating to date archaeological remains, given the proliferation of other dateable material across the continent from this period onwards. Given that this variable underpins this paper’s primary analyses and main conclusions, I would expect some critical discussion in the main text that outlines the well-known and strongly debated limitations of using SPDs for paleodemographic inference, though this is missing. This would then help justify the decision to cut off the analyses at 2.5 cal k BP, which at the moment does not feel sufficiently justified in the text.

> **Response.** We retain archaeological SPDs as validated proxies for regional human population changes, while agreeing that they are not direct population censuses. They are shaped by the survival and discovery of archaeological material, the history and intensity of research, laboratory dating practices, and the structure of the radiocarbon calibration curve. These influences vary among continental groups, regions, and periods and become particularly important near the younger boundary of this study. The regional distributions of dates and SPDs showed that 2.0 ka BP is the youngest common 500-year boundary at which a broad comparison remains supportable. We use it as a practical limit for this global historical comparison, not as a universal date after which SPDs cease to be informative.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Methods and Discussion now describe SPDs as archaeological histories whose interpretation depends on preservation and research practice. Supplementary Fig. S2 shows the regional coverage that informed the 2.0 ka BP boundary, and the article does not extend the principal conclusion into younger periods.

Notwithstanding these comments, of most concern to me is the different spatial scales of the respective variables used in these analyses. The relevant source area of pollen for any given extracted fossil pollen sequence varies from meters up to tens of kilometers (rarely hundreds of km), depending on the deposition environment, location, etc. However, the authors pull radiocarbon dates from either 250km or 500km surrounding a pollen record extraction location to build their SPDs. These scales are vastly different and it is perhaps not surprising that PAPs from, for example, a bog site with a pollen source area in the order of hundreds of meters are not associated with SPDs built from radiocarbon dates pulled from within 250 or 500km but that they are associated with paleoclimate estimates for the actual location of a pollen record. In principle, either (i) a dynamic radius for retrieving radiocarbon dates per pollen record could be used (based on each record’s pollen source area), (ii) these analyses could be run regionally (using averages across PAPs and predictor variables) or (iii), at the very least, a sensitivity analysis should be run that restricts the analyses to those records with the largest pollen source areas, with SPDs built using a radius for radiocarbon dates that is at least equal in order of magnitude to it.

> **Response.** We agree that the pollen and archaeological evidence describe landscapes at very different scales. Pollen deposited in a small bog may chiefly reflect vegetation within a few kilometres or less, whereas an SPD assembled within 250 or 500 km describes a much broader archaeological landscape. Ideally, the archaeological neighbourhood would be tailored to the source area of each pollen sequence. This is not possible here because basin dimensions, depositional settings, and estimates of pollen source area are unavailable or inconsistent for much of the global compilation. We therefore compared the same pollen sequences using archaeological dates drawn from 250 and 500 km. Among `r format(radius_spatial_n, big.mark = ",")` sequences available for both comparisons, `r radius_spatial_reversals` changed from a climate-dominant to a human-dominant result, or vice versa; among `r radius_temporal_n` continental-group time comparisons, `r radius_temporal_reversals` changed ordering. The median change in the spatial climate–human balance was `r sprintf("%.3f", radius_spatial_delta_median)`. This shows that the chosen archaeological neighbourhood affects some individual results, while leaving the broad pattern intact. Because even 250 km greatly exceeds the pollen source area of many sites, this comparison does not remove the mismatch. We have accordingly restricted the conclusion to broad regional patterns and emphasised that individual sites retain their own ecological and land-use histories.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Methods now explain why proximity to a pollen site must be balanced against the number of archaeological dates available. Supplementary Figs. S8 and S37–S38 and Supplementary Table S9 present the 250 and 500 km comparison. The Discussion explains why it cannot substitute for site-specific pollen-source estimates.

The matched spatial comparison of archaeological search radii is reproduced below. It tests the operational radius choice; neither radius represents a measured pollen-source area.

### Human events variable

Even by itself, the development of this variable represents a major undertaking and whilst I appreciate the substantial effort, I find the decomposition of continuous human change into categorical events represented by a binary variable overly simplistic and almost certain not to capture diverse changes across the PAPs considered here. I also find there to be a lack of description and justification of the method. Which experts were asked? Why were these experts asked? Who do they represent? Why and how were these events chosen? By whom? What were the exact criteria used for each event * region considered? Indeed, for Central and South America, the authors use an established index from the literature, which underlines the extent of the work required for the development of indices such as these for individual continents, let alone for all continents as is attempted here.

The reductive nature of the index is exemplified best for North America, for which the authors provide three event categories: No Evidence of Impact, First Cultivation and European Settlement. For many Indigenous North American peoples, cultivating domesticated plant types remained supplementary to a much broader focus on foraging wild foods (both plant and animal) over the Holocene. Wild foods were often foraged with the substantial assistance of fire, which was used extensively across the continent before, during and after cultivation of domestic crops. According to this index, there was no human impact in North America before First cultivation, which is certainly untrue. Indigenous groups across North America have impacted vegetative communities over the entire Holocene and into the Pleistocene both directly, through burning, and indirectly, through the removal of the largest animals. Both of these would have strongly impacted vegetative communities, but their effects are entirely missed by the coarse categories here. It would be a vast amount of work to develop a pollen-based index of human impact for all regions globally that was transparent and not overly reductive. I do not believe that, in its present form, the inclusion of this binary variable adds to this work and I would simply remove it and curtail the analyses at the end of the period of SPD relevance, however defined.

> **Response.** We agree that a binary event chronology cannot capture the continuity and diversity of past human land use. Clearance, grazing, cultivation, burning, and settlement varied in form, duration, intensity, and ecological consequence among regions. We have therefore removed “No Evidence of Impact” as an interpretation: absence of a recorded event means only that the specified pollen indicator was not identified. Nevertheless, we retain the chronology as secondary historical evidence because it brings locally interpreted indications of land use into a study otherwise dependent on broad archaeological SPDs, includes some younger observations, and allows us to ask whether the climate–human comparison changes when human activity is represented differently. Its partial dependence on the pollen sequence is stated explicitly, and it is not presented as independent confirmation.

> The comparison is limited to places and periods for which an expert chronology was actually available: `r event_spatial_n` pollen sequences in the spatial analysis and `r event_temporal_n` continental-group–age combinations in the temporal analysis. Adding or substituting the event evidence changed estimates in both directions. This variability is historically informative because it shows that the inferred human contribution depends in part on the archive used to represent past activity. It does not extend the principal SPD conclusion beyond 2.0 ka BP. John Birks and Hilary Birks assessed Europe and North America; John Birks and Kuber Bhatta assessed Asia; and Simon Haberle and Annika Herbert assessed Oceania. They were chosen for regional palaeoecological and pollen-analytical expertise. The Central and South American indicators follow the published regional synthesis. The Methods section describes how the diagrams were assessed, and Supplementary Table S4 summarises the event categories, and the Methods retain the detailed regional detection criteria from the submitted version.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The event chronology is now presented as a complementary historical perspective rather than evidence equal to the archaeological SPD. The Methods identify the experts and regional indicators, the Discussion addresses the incompleteness and partial circularity of the evidence, and the Supplementary Information compares results based on SPDs, events, and both sources together.

We reproduce the matched comparison of human-activity proxies so that the effect of retaining the event chronology can be assessed directly. These results use observed event chronologies and do not treat an undetected event as absence of human activity.

### Statistical analyses

Firstly, I cannot see a summary of the total variance explained by the models here. This is of crucial importance because if the models explain a very small amount of the total variation in the data, then it would be difficult to say that humans/climate are most/not important drivers of the PAPs, in my view. These should be added as a Supplementary table and summarised in some way - perhaps across records, by region - as an Extended Data Figure.

> **Response.** We agree that the strength of the ecological interpretation depends on how much variation the models explain. For the `r format(spatial_controlled_n, big.mark = ",")` pollen sequences in the principal spatial analysis, total adjusted $R^2$ is `r sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", spatial_mean_adjusted_r2_controlled, spatial_controlled_fit_ci[1], spatial_controlled_fit_ci[2])` (mean, 95% CI). The sequence-level distribution is `r sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", spatial_median_adjusted_r2, spatial_q1_adjusted_r2_controlled, spatial_q3_adjusted_r2_controlled)` (median, interquartile range). Supplementary Fig. S31 shows how explanatory power varies among continental groups and regions, because a global average can conceal pollen sequences for which climate and human activity account for little of the observed history. Supplementary Table S5 separately reports the larger set of `r format(spatial_available_n, big.mark = ",")` sequences for which the original comparison of climatic and human contributions could be estimated.

> During revision, we also corrected how the separate climatic and human contributions were extracted. The revised article retains the signed estimates, uses non-negative values only for the principal visual summary, and reports a further comparison that omits models with negative components. Climate had the larger estimated contribution under each treatment, although the numerical values differed. We stress that these contributions divide the variation explained by a model and must not be read as proportions of all change in the pollen assemblage.

> **Changes in the revised article.** The Results now report overall model fit alongside the comparison of climate and human activity. Supplementary figures and tables show its geographical distribution, its relationship to the estimated contributions, and the effect of alternative treatments of shared or negative explanatory variation.

The model-fit distribution and the comparison of extraction profiles are reproduced below. Total adjusted $R^2$ describes complete-model fit, whereas the profiles show alternative allocations of the fitted component.

![](../figures/supplementary-figure-22-hvarpart-profiles.png){width=90% fig-alt="Supplementary Fig. S4: signed, zero-truncated, and exclude-negative HVarPart profiles."}

**Supplementary Fig. S4 (reproduced). HVarPart extraction profiles.** Signed, zero-truncated, and exclude-negative summaries are compared for their respective eligible analysis subsets; these allocations are distinct from total adjusted $R^2$.

{{< pagebreak >}}

Secondly, temporal and spatial autocorrelation do not seem to be accounted for in these models, and their effects not checked for. These effects potentially confound model inferences and thus either an explanation as to why they were not included needs to be added to the methods, or some additional variables need to be added to the models. This is likely of most importance to those analyses in Fig 2 where there will undoubtedly be a substantial trend component to the PAPs over the long period considered.

> **Response.** We agree that ecological observations close together in time or space are not independent. Long-term succession and directional change can make neighbouring levels within a pollen sequence resemble one another, while shared geography can produce similar assemblages among nearby sites. The principal analysis of individual sequences now accounts for temporal structure, and the continental-group analysis through time accounts for spatial structure among sites. We also examine remaining spatial pattern in the residuals, repeat analyses using more widely spaced sequences, and test whether the broad result depends on any single continental group or region. These checks retain the general predominance of climate, while showing that some individual estimates remain uncertain or sensitive to analytical choices.

> **Changes in the revised article.** Figs. 3 and 4 now present the analyses that account for temporal or spatial structure. The Methods describe these controls, and the Supplementary Information reports checks for remaining geographical pattern, the influence of closely spaced sites, and the effect of excluding individual continental groups or regions.

We reproduce the residual spatial-dependence and thinning diagnostics because they show what the controls changed and what geographical structure remains.

{{< pagebreak >}}

![](../figures/supplementary-figure-31-moran.png){width=90% fig-alt="Supplementary Fig. S6: residual spatial autocorrelation before and after control."}

**Supplementary Fig. S6 (reproduced). Residual spatial dependence.** Moran diagnostics compare spatial pattern before and after control in eligible spatial subsets; residual clustering is not assumed to disappear completely.

{{< pagebreak >}}

![](../figures/supplementary-figure-32-thinning.png){width=90% fig-alt="Supplementary Fig. S34: spatial thinning at 250 and 500 km."}

**Supplementary Fig. S34 (reproduced). Spatial thinning.** Repeatedly retaining more widely separated sequences tests whether densely sampled places determine the aggregate climate–human balance.
